## Solution

Consider the complex exponential $e^{-ie^{i\theta}}$. Expanding:

$$e^{-ie^{i\theta}} = e^{-i(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)} = e^{\sin\theta - i\cos\theta} = e^{\sin\theta}\bigl(\cos(\cos\theta) - i\sin(\cos\theta)\bigr).$$

Taking the real part:

$$\operatorname{Re}\!\left(e^{-ie^{i\theta}}\right) = e^{\sin\theta}\cos(\cos\theta).$$

Therefore our integral equals

$$I = \operatorname{Re}\int_0^{2\pi} e^{-ie^{i\theta}}\,d\theta.$$

Now expand the integrand as a power series in $e^{i\theta}$:

$$e^{-ie^{i\theta}} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-i)^n}{n!}\,e^{in\theta}.$$

Since this series converges uniformly in $\theta$ (it is dominated by $\sum \frac{1}{n!}=e$), we may integrate term by term:

$$\int_0^{2\pi} e^{-ie^{i\theta}}\,d\theta = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-i)^n}{n!}\int_0^{2\pi} e^{in\theta}\,d\theta.$$

For $n\neq 0$, $\int_0^{2\pi} e^{in\theta}\,d\theta = 0$. For $n=0$, the integral equals $2\pi$. Hence every term vanishes except the $n=0$ term:

$$\int_0^{2\pi} e^{-ie^{i\theta}}\,d\theta = \frac{(-i)^0}{0!}\cdot 2\pi = 2\pi.$$

This value is purely real, so taking the real part leaves it unchanged:

$$I = \operatorname{Re}(2\pi) = 2\pi.$$

$$\boxed{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi} \exp(\sin \theta)\,\cos(\cos \theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 2\pi.}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
